script.opening: "Hello doctor. I’ve been so stiff and sore in my shoulders and hips for weeks now — mornings are dreadful, I can barely lift my arms to brush my hair or get out of bed, it takes a couple of hours to loosen up. My friend had something similar, polymyalgia, and steroids sorted her right out. Could I have a course of those? Oh, and I’ve had a bit of a headache this week but that’s neither here nor there."

facts.text: If explored: bilateral shoulder- and pelvic-girdle pain and prolonged morning stiffness (>45 min, often hours) for ~6 weeks, age >50, difficulty with overhead tasks and rising — a classic polymyalgia rheumatica presentation, typically steroid-responsive.

CRITICAL, on direct questioning (she dismisses these): NEW unilateral headache, SCALP TENDERNESS (hurts to brush hair / rest head on pillow), and JAW CLAUDICATION (aching in the jaw on chewing). These are giant cell arteritis features. GCA can cause sudden, irreversible BLINDNESS — it is a medical emergency. PMR and GCA overlap: some people with PMR have or go on to develop GCA.

If asked: no visual loss, blurring or double vision so far — but this is the window to prevent it. Visual symptoms (amaurosis, diplopia) would be a same-day sight-threatening emergency. She treats the absence of visual symptoms as reassurance; it is the chance to act before they occur.

HIDDEN AGENDA — she is downplaying the headache/jaw symptoms partly because she’s fixed on the PMR/steroid answer her friend had, and partly STEROID FEAR: she’s heard steroids cause weight gain, brittle bones, "moon face" and is privately reluctant to take a long course, hoping for a short one. She also cares for her husband with dementia and can’t afford to be unwell. The jaw/scalp clues nearly go unspoken.

Officially: a short steroid course for the stiffness. What she needs: recognition that the new headache + scalp tenderness + jaw claudication signal GCA — a sight-threatening emergency needing HIGH-dose steroids immediately and urgent GCA fast-track referral (BSR 2020: specialist review ideally the same working day, and in all cases within 3 working days) — plus honest steroid counselling and carer support.

ice.ideas: She has polymyalgia like her friend; a course of steroids will fix the stiffness.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — steroid fear (weight gain, bones, "moon face") so she’s hoping for a short course; and she’s a carer for her husband with dementia and can’t afford to be ill, so she’s minimising the headache/jaw symptoms.
ice.expectations: A short steroid course for the stiffness. What she actually needs: recognition of GCA red flags, urgent HIGH-dose steroids and same-day referral to prevent blindness, plus honest steroid counselling and carer support.

cues: Girdle pain + prolonged morning stiffness >45min at 72 — classic PMR.
"A headache, but that’s neither here nor there" + scalp tenderness + jaw ache on chewing — GCA red flags she’s dismissing; sight-threatening.
Fixed on a short steroid course / steroid fear — and a carer who can’t afford to be ill; the reasons she’s minimising.

checkpoints.text: Recognises the PMR picture (bilateral girdle pain, prolonged morning stiffness >45 min, age >50) AND — critically — actively asks about and identifies the GIANT CELL ARTERITIS red flags: new unilateral headache, scalp tenderness, and jaw claudication
Recognises GCA as a SIGHT-THREATENING EMERGENCY: explains it can cause sudden irreversible blindness, and that the absence of visual loss now is the window to PREVENT it, not reassurance

Starts HIGH-dose corticosteroid IMMEDIATELY for suspected GCA (BSR 2020: prednisolone 40–60 mg once daily, started by the GP the same day; IV methylprednisolone via same-day ophthalmology if any visual symptoms) WITHOUT waiting for tests, and arranges urgent referral to the GCA fast-track pathway (BSR 2020: specialist review ideally the same working day and in all cases within 3 working days; same-day ophthalmology if visual) and urgent bloods (ESR/CRP) + temporal artery biopsy/ultrasound within 1 week of starting steroids — treatment must not be delayed for investigations

Distinguishes from isolated PMR (which uses lower-dose steroids: prednisolone 15 mg daily, BSR/BHPR 2010) and knows that visual symptoms (amaurosis fugax, diplopia, visual loss) escalate to a SAME-DAY ophthalmology emergency with IV steroids

Counsels steroids honestly and safely: necessity here (sight preservation) vs the patient’s fears, the prolonged taper GCA requires, and steroid safety-netting (bone protection started at the same time without waiting for DXA, NOGG 2024; consider a PPI, BSR 2020; glucose and BP; Steroid Emergency Card, NatPSA/2020/005; sick-day rules, NICE NG243; not stopping abruptly)

Picks up the dismissed headache/jaw clues rather than accepting the PMR self-diagnosis, and explores them actively; addresses the steroid fear and the carer pressure with empathy so she accepts urgent treatment
Conveys the seriousness (possible blindness) without inducing panic, and supports her as a carer — recognising she needs to stay well for her husband, which is a reason TO treat, not avoid it

Safety-nets emphatically: start steroids now; if ANY visual symptoms (loss, blurring, double vision) develop → same-day eye emergency/999; urgent referral and bloods arranged; steroid safety-net and carer support; documents and follows up

worked.txt: "You’re right that the shoulder and hip stiffness sounds like polymyalgia, and yes, steroids help that hugely. But before I prescribe — you mentioned a headache as if it were nothing, and I need to take that seriously. Can I ask: is the headache on one side? Is your scalp tender, say when you brush your hair? And does your jaw ache when you chew? …"

"Thank you — those answers matter a great deal. Polymyalgia sometimes comes with a related condition affecting the blood vessels around the temple, called giant cell arteritis. The reason I can’t treat it as ‘just stiffness’ is that, untreated, it can cause sudden loss of sight — and that can be permanent. The fact you can still see fine is exactly why we act NOW, to keep it that way."

"So I’m not going to wait for tests. I want you to start a higher dose of steroid today — straight away — because protecting your sight can’t wait for blood results or scans. I’ll arrange urgent blood tests and an urgent specialist review as well — ideally today, and within three working days at most — but the steroid starts now. This is the one situation where we treat first and confirm after."

"And this is the most important thing I’ll say: if you get ANY change in your vision — blurring, loss, a curtain coming down, double vision — that is a 999 / eye-emergency, the same day, no waiting. Don’t ‘see how it goes’ with your eyes, ever, with this."

"I know steroids worry people — the weight, the bones, the moon face — and I won’t pretend there are no downsides on a longer course. But weigh that against your eyesight: this is a clear case where the benefit massively outweighs the risk. I’ll start bone protection straight away, think with you about stomach protection, give you a steroid emergency card, and we’ll bring the dose down slowly and safely over time. You won’t be on high doses forever."

"You also told me you look after your husband — which is even more reason to keep yourself well and your sight intact, so let’s treat this properly. I’ll sort the urgent referral and bloods today, and some support so you’re not doing it all alone. Start the steroid now, never stop it suddenly, and ring 999 for any visual change. I’ll follow this up closely with you."

f.learning: Polymyalgia rheumatica (bilateral girdle pain, prolonged morning stiffness, age >50, steroid-responsive) carries a sight-threatening companion: giant cell arteritis. The examinable skill is to actively ask about and act on the GCA red flags — new unilateral headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication (and visual symptoms) — even when the patient dismisses them, because GCA can cause sudden, irreversible blindness. The absence of visual loss now is the window to PREVENT it. Suspected GCA is treated with HIGH-dose corticosteroid IMMEDIATELY (BSR 2020: prednisolone 40–60 mg once daily; IV methylprednisolone via same-day ophthalmology if any visual symptoms) WITHOUT waiting for ESR/CRP or temporal artery biopsy, plus urgent GCA fast-track referral (BSR 2020: ideally the same working day, in all cases within 3 working days); any visual symptom is a same-day ophthalmology emergency. This contrasts with isolated PMR (prednisolone 15 mg daily, BSR/BHPR 2010). The hidden agenda is steroid fear (hoping for a short course) and carer pressure driving her to minimise the headache/jaw clues; counsel steroids honestly (necessity for sight, prolonged taper, bone protection per NOGG 2024, a PPI considered rather than routine per BSR 2020, Steroid Emergency Card, sick-day rules per NICE NG243), support her as a carer, and safety-net visual symptoms emphatically.

knowledge.guideline: BSR GCA guideline (Mackie et al., 2020) · BSR/BHPR PMR guideline (Dasgupta et al., 2010) · NOGG 2024 · NatPSA/2020/005 Steroid Emergency Card · NICE NG243 (2024) · BNF
knowledge.summary: Girdle pain and long morning stiffness at 72 fits polymyalgia, but a new headache, scalp tenderness and jaw pain on chewing mean suspected giant cell arteritis. Start high-dose prednisolone today and refer on the GCA fast-track pathway; tests must not delay treatment.

points.t: BSR/BHPR 2010: age over 50, bilateral shoulder and/or pelvic girdle aching with inflammatory morning stiffness for 2 weeks or more and raised inflammatory markers. Baseline bloods before steroids: FBC, ESR or CRP, U&E, LFT, bone profile, protein electrophoresis, TSH, CK, rheumatoid factor and urine dipstick. Isolated PMR starts at prednisolone 15 mg daily.

PMR and GCA overlap. Ask every patient with PMR symptoms about new headache (often temporal, one-sided), scalp tenderness, jaw or tongue claudication, visual disturbance and systemic upset. Jaw claudication is a high-risk feature.

BSR 2020: suspected GCA without visual loss — prednisolone 40–60 mg once daily, started by the GP the same day. Acute or intermittent visual loss — IV methylprednisolone (500 mg–1 g daily for up to 3 days) via same-day ophthalmology; do not delay oral steroid if IV is not immediately possible.

BSR 2020: refer urgently to the local GCA fast-track service — specialist review ideally the same working day and in all cases within 3 working days. Ultrasound of the temporal and axillary arteries (ideally before or within 72 hours of the first dose) and/or temporal artery biopsy (at least 1 cm), arranged urgently through the pathway, because steroids reduce test sensitivity. Tests must never delay treatment.

NOGG 2024: starting prednisolone 7.5 mg/day or more for 3 months or longer in a postmenopausal woman — start bone protection at the same time, without waiting for DXA. BSR 2020: gastroprotection according to GI risk, not routinely. NatPSA/2020/005: Steroid Emergency Card for 5 mg or more for 4 weeks or longer; sick-day rules per NICE NG243. Monitor glucose and BP. Never stop suddenly.

BSR 2020: hold the starting dose until symptoms and inflammatory markers have settled, then taper slowly to an individualised plan; the course commonly lasts 12–24 months. Symptoms usually respond within 1–7 days; no response should prompt a rethink.

dg.d: Open question on the phone after an identity check; let her give the whole story, including the headache she dismissed.
Caring role for her husband with dementia; who covers him for appointments; the impact of the stiffness on daily tasks.
Same-day bloods (FBC, ESR/CRP, U&E, LFT, bone profile, glucose) without delaying steroids; fast-track referral for ultrasound or biopsy.
PMR alone versus PMR with GCA; PMR mimics (myeloma, other inflammatory arthritis) kept in mind.
Asked directly about scalp tenderness, jaw claudication and visual symptoms; knew visual loss means same-day ophthalmology and IV steroid.
Stated suspected GCA with PMR and explained it in plain words — sight is at risk, normal vision now is the window.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Prednisolone 40–60 mg started today (not the PMR dose), fast-track referral, bone protection, Steroid Emergency Card and a slow taper explained.
Hypertension and glucose monitoring on steroids; bone protection per NOGG 2024; gastroprotection considered; carer’s assessment offered.
Named visual symptoms as a 999 emergency, never stop steroids suddenly, and a GP call the next day.

Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “a bit of a headache, neither here nor there” and turned it into specific GCA questions.
Idea (polymyalgia like her friend); concern (steroid side effects, being unable to care for her husband); expectation (a short course).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.

Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, is that Mrs Vance? It’s Dr Lee from the surgery. Can I just check your date of birth? … Thank you. Is now a good time to talk? … You’ve had a rough few weeks by the sound of it — tell me what’s been going on.
model.why: Confirms identity on the phone and opens with the patient’s story

model.text: Oh, it’s this stiffness, doctor. Shoulders and hips, for about six weeks. Mornings are dreadful — a couple of hours before I can lift my arms to brush my hair. My friend had polymyalgia and steroids sorted her right out. Could I have a course of those? Oh, and I’ve had a bit of a headache this week, but that’s neither here nor there.

That sounds really hard, and you may well be right about polymyalgia. I do want to get you something that helps. Before I prescribe, I’d like to ask a few questions — including about that headache — and then we’ll agree a plan. Is that all right?
model.why: Accepts her idea as plausible but keeps the headache on the agenda

model.text: Yes, of course.
Tell me about the stiffness first. Is it both sides? And do you feel unwell in yourself — any weight loss, fevers or sweats?
model.why: Confirms the girdle pattern and screens systemic features

model.text: Both sides, yes. Getting out of bed is a performance. I’ve been tired, but I put that down to everything.
Now that headache — you brushed it off, but I’d like to hear about it. Where is it, and is it new for you?
model.why: Picks up the dismissed cue rather than letting it pass

model.text: It’s on this side, by my temple. It’s new — I don’t really get headaches.
Thank you. A few specific questions. Is your scalp tender — say when you brush your hair or lay your head on the pillow? And does your jaw ache when you chew, easing when you stop?
model.why: Asks directly about scalp tenderness and jaw claudication

model.text: Now you mention it, yes — the pillow is sore on that side. And my jaw aches halfway through a meal. I thought it was my teeth.
That’s really important, I’m glad you told me. Any change at all in your eyesight — blurring, double vision, or a patch or curtain of vision going, even briefly?
model.why: Screens for visual symptoms, which change the urgency

model.text: No, my eyes are fine. So that’s good, isn’t it?
It’s good that your sight is fine — and I’ll explain why that matters in a moment. You mentioned wanting a course of steroids. What have you heard about them?
model.why: Explores her expectation and what sits behind it

model.text: Well, my friend said a short course. But I’ve heard about the weight, the moon face, the bones. I don’t want to be on them for ages. And I look after my husband — he has dementia — so I really can’t be ill.
That’s a lot to be holding, and it makes sense you want this over quickly. Thank you for telling me about your husband — I’ll make sure the plan works around him.
model.why: Names the steroid fear and the carer pressure before the explanation

model.text: Here’s my honest view. The stiffness does sound like polymyalgia. But a new headache on one side, a tender scalp and jaw ache when you chew point to a related condition called giant cell arteritis — inflammation in the blood vessels around the temple. Untreated, it can cause sudden and permanent loss of sight. Your eyesight being fine now is exactly why we act today — to keep it that way.
model.why: Explains GCA and reframes normal vision as the window to protect it

model.text: Goodness. I had no idea. I thought it was just a headache.

That’s why I asked. So I don’t want to wait for tests. I’m going to prescribe steroid tablets today at a much higher dose than your friend had — that’s what protects the eyes. I’ll send it to your pharmacy now, and I’d like you to start it as soon as you collect it.
model.why: Starts high-dose prednisolone the same day without waiting for results

model.text: Today? But what about the side effects?

It’s a fair question. There are downsides on a longer course and I won’t pretend otherwise. But here the balance is clear — your sight comes first. I’ll protect your bones and stomach, check your sugar and blood pressure, and give you a steroid card. We’ll bring the dose down slowly once things settle — not all at once.
model.why: Addresses the steroid fear honestly and weighs it against sight

model.text: I’m also referring you today to the hospital’s rapid-access service for this condition. They aim to see people within a few days, often the same day, and they’ll arrange a scan or a small biopsy of the artery to confirm it. I’d like bloods today as well. Can you get to the surgery this afternoon?
model.why: Arranges fast-track referral and same-day bloods alongside treatment

model.text: I’d need someone to sit with my husband. I’m not sure who.
Let’s solve that together. Our team can look at who could help for the appointments, and I’d like to arrange a carer’s assessment so you have support if you’re unwell. Would that be okay?
model.why: Builds the carer constraint into the plan so it happens

model.text: Yes. I hadn’t thought about what happens if I’m the one who’s poorly.
That’s exactly why it matters. Staying well and keeping your sight is how you keep looking after him.
model.why: Frames treatment as protecting her role as a carer

model.text: The most important thing I’ll say today: if you get any change in your vision — blurring, double vision, or part of your sight going, even for a few minutes — that is an emergency. Call 999 or go straight to A&E and say you’re being treated for giant cell arteritis. Don’t wait to see if it passes.
model.why: Specific visual safety-net with an action and a phrase to use

model.text: I understand. Any change in my eyes, 999.
Exactly. Never stop the steroid suddenly, and carry the card. I’ll ring you tomorrow to check you’ve started and to go through the bloods. Can you tell me back the three things you’re doing today?
Start the tablets, bloods this afternoon, and 999 if my eyes change. And the hospital will call.
Perfect. You did the right thing ringing. Anything else you wanted to ask?
model.why: Checks understanding and shares the floor

model.text: No, thank you, doctor. I’m glad I mentioned the headache now.

social.t: She cares for her husband with dementia. Appointments, a possible biopsy and feeling unwell on treatment all need cover for him — plan it now or she will not attend.
Weight, mood, sleep and appetite change on high doses. Practical support and honest expectations improve adherence over a long taper.

legal.t: Any carer who appears to have support needs is entitled to a local authority carer’s assessment. Her husband can have a needs assessment and contingency planning if she becomes unwell.
No action needed while vision is normal. If GCA causes visual loss or a visual field defect, she must tell the DVLA and meet the Group 1 eyesight standard before driving.

professional.t: Starting high-dose steroid before confirmation is correct practice here (BSR 2020). Document the red flags, the dose, the referral and the safety-net advice given (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).
A phone call cannot examine the temporal artery or check acuity. Recognise the limit and bring examination and bloods forward the same day rather than deferring treatment.

community.t: PMRGCAuk (patient charity) for information and peer support; local carers’ centre and Carers UK; Dementia UK Admiral Nurses for her husband’s care planning.

redFlags: New one-sided headache, scalp tenderness, jaw or tongue claudication — suspected GCA
Any visual symptom (transient blurring, double vision, field loss) — same-day ophthalmology and IV steroid
Weight loss, night sweats, bone pain — consider PMR mimics such as myeloma
psychosocial: Sole carer for a husband with dementia — who covers him for appointments and if she is unwell
Steroid fears drawn from a friend’s experience and what she has read
Impact of the stiffness on dressing, washing and caring tasks
ice: Idea: “It’s polymyalgia, like my friend had.”
Concern: steroid side effects, and not being able to look after her husband
Expectation: a short course of steroids for the stiffness

playbook.diagnosis: Be clear that this is suspected giant cell arteritis alongside polymyalgia: “The stiffness fits polymyalgia, but the headache, tender scalp and jaw ache point to inflammation in the arteries that can threaten your sight — so we treat it today.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of the blood vessels to your eye as a hosepipe that’s getting inflamed and narrowed. At the moment water is still getting through — your sight is fine. The steroid calms the inflammation before the hose is squeezed shut.”

management.reflectIce: “You were hoping for a short course, and you need to stay well for your husband. Treating this properly now is exactly what keeps you able to look after him.”
management.psychosocial: Arrange cover for her husband for the bloods and the specialist visit; offer a carer’s assessment and a contingency plan; give written steroid information to take away.
sharedPlan: Prednisolone 40–60 mg daily started today; fast-track GCA referral; same-day bloods
Bone protection, consider a PPI, Steroid Emergency Card, glucose and BP monitoring
Slow taper led by the specialist team; carer’s assessment and cover for appointments
safetyNet: Any visual change — 999 or A&E, say “giant cell arteritis”
Never stop steroids suddenly; sick-day rules; GP call tomorrow

pitfalls.intro: This station is not about knowing that GCA exists. It is failed on accepting the patient’s label, delaying steroids for tests, and ignoring the two things she is really worried about.

items.fail: Accepting “it’s polymyalgia” and prescribing 15 mg without asking about the headache.
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information to make a safe assessment.” She mentioned the headache once, then dismissed it — that is the test.
items.fix: Go back to it explicitly: side, newness, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual symptoms.

items.fail: Recognising GCA but waiting for ESR and CRP before starting steroids.
items.why: BSR 2020: start prednisolone 40–60 mg on clinical suspicion; tests must not delay treatment.
items.fix: “The steroid starts today; the tests follow.” Bloods the same day, and a fast-track referral.

items.fail: Starting high-dose steroid with no bone protection, steroid card or taper plan.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” NOGG 2024 advises bone protection from the start in this group; NatPSA/2020/005 requires a Steroid Emergency Card.
items.fix: Name bone protection, consider a PPI, give the card, and say the dose comes down slowly.

items.fail: Saying “don’t worry about side effects” when she raises moon face and bones.
items.why: “Does not respond to the patient’s concerns.” Brushing off an informed fear loses the trust needed for a year-long course.
items.fix: Acknowledge the downsides honestly, then weigh them openly against permanent loss of sight.

items.fail: Never returning to her husband after she mentions his dementia.
items.why: The carer role is why she is minimising. If nobody can sit with him, she will not attend.
items.fix: “Who could be with your husband this afternoon?” Offer a carer’s assessment and help with cover.

items.fail: A vague close — “ring us if things get worse”.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is standard failing feedback, and here it risks her sight.
items.fix: “Any change in your vision, even brief — 999 or A&E, and say giant cell arteritis.” Then teach-back and a dated call.

timeMap.d: She opens with the diagnosis and the request, and throws away the headache. Note it and agree an agenda that includes it.
Girdle pattern and morning stiffness, systemic features, then the GCA questions: temporal headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, any visual symptoms.
Steroid fear (weight, bones, moon face) and her husband with dementia. Name both before you explain anything.
Suspected GCA — sight at risk. Prednisolone 40–60 mg today, fast-track referral, same-day bloods, bone and stomach protection, steroid card. Solve who sits with her husband.
Any visual change is a 999 call. Never stop steroids suddenly. GP call tomorrow. Teach-back of the three actions for today.

wordPics.pass: Asks the GCA questions and recognises the red flags; starts high-dose prednisolone today and refers on the fast-track pathway; arranges bloods; gives a clear visual-loss safety-net and mentions steroid side effects.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: turns her dismissed headache into the key finding without alarming her; explains why normal eyesight is the reason to act now; weighs steroid fears honestly with bone protection and a steroid card; builds her husband’s care into the plan with a carer’s assessment; closes with teach-back and a next-day call.

avoid.dont: “It sounds like polymyalgia — I’ll send you some steroids like your friend had.”
avoid.instead: “Before I prescribe, tell me more about that headache — is your scalp sore, and does your jaw ache when you chew?”
avoid.why: Treating GCA at the PMR dose, or missing it, is the dangerous fail in this station.

avoid.dont: “Let’s get some bloods first and I’ll decide on steroids when they’re back.”
avoid.instead: “I don’t want to wait for tests — the steroid starts today, and the tests follow.”
avoid.why: BSR 2020: tests must never delay treatment in suspected GCA.

avoid.dont: “Don’t worry about the side effects, it’s only for a short while.”
avoid.instead: “This will be a longer course, and I’ll protect your bones and stomach — but your sight comes first.”
avoid.why: False reassurance about duration undermines trust when the taper takes a year or more.

SCA_MODELS.text: Oh, it’s this stiffness, doctor. Shoulders and hips, for about six weeks. Mornings are dreadful — a couple of hours before I can lift my arms to brush my hair. My friend had polymyalgia and steroids sorted her right out. Could I have a course of those? Oh, and I’ve had a bit of a headache this week, but that’s neither here nor there.

That sounds really hard, and you may well be right about polymyalgia. I do want to get you something that helps. Before I prescribe, I’d like to ask a few questions — including about that headache — and then we’ll agree a plan. Is that all right?
SCA_MODELS.why: Accepts her idea as plausible but keeps the headache on the agenda

SCA_MODELS.text: Yes, of course.
Tell me about the stiffness first. Is it both sides? And do you feel unwell in yourself — any weight loss, fevers or sweats?
SCA_MODELS.why: Confirms the girdle pattern and screens systemic features

SCA_MODELS.text: Both sides, yes. Getting out of bed is a performance. I’ve been tired, but I put that down to everything.
Now that headache — you brushed it off, but I’d like to hear about it. Where is it, and is it new for you?
SCA_MODELS.why: Picks up the dismissed cue rather than letting it pass

SCA_MODELS.text: It’s on this side, by my temple. It’s new — I don’t really get headaches.
Thank you. A few specific questions. Is your scalp tender — say when you brush your hair or lay your head on the pillow? And does your jaw ache when you chew, easing when you stop?
SCA_MODELS.why: Asks directly about scalp tenderness and jaw claudication

SCA_MODELS.text: Now you mention it, yes — the pillow is sore on that side. And my jaw aches halfway through a meal. I thought it was my teeth.
That’s really important, I’m glad you told me. Any change at all in your eyesight — blurring, double vision, or a patch or curtain of vision going, even briefly?
SCA_MODELS.why: Screens for visual symptoms, which change the urgency

SCA_MODELS.text: No, my eyes are fine. So that’s good, isn’t it?
It’s good that your sight is fine — and I’ll explain why that matters in a moment. You mentioned wanting a course of steroids. What have you heard about them?
SCA_MODELS.why: Explores her expectation and what sits behind it

SCA_MODELS.text: Well, my friend said a short course. But I’ve heard about the weight, the moon face, the bones. I don’t want to be on them for ages. And I look after my husband — he has dementia — so I really can’t be ill.
That’s a lot to be holding, and it makes sense you want this over quickly. Thank you for telling me about your husband — I’ll make sure the plan works around him.
SCA_MODELS.why: Names the steroid fear and the carer pressure before the explanation

SCA_MODELS.text: Here’s my honest view. The stiffness does sound like polymyalgia. But a new headache on one side, a tender scalp and jaw ache when you chew point to a related condition called giant cell arteritis — inflammation in the blood vessels around the temple. Untreated, it can cause sudden and permanent loss of sight. Your eyesight being fine now is exactly why we act today — to keep it that way.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains GCA and reframes normal vision as the window to protect it

SCA_MODELS.text: Goodness. I had no idea. I thought it was just a headache.

That’s why I asked. So I don’t want to wait for tests. I’m going to prescribe steroid tablets today at a much higher dose than your friend had — that’s what protects the eyes. I’ll send it to your pharmacy now, and I’d like you to start it as soon as you collect it.
SCA_MODELS.why: Starts high-dose prednisolone the same day without waiting for results

SCA_MODELS.text: Today? But what about the side effects?

It’s a fair question. There are downsides on a longer course and I won’t pretend otherwise. But here the balance is clear — your sight comes first. I’ll protect your bones and stomach, check your sugar and blood pressure, and give you a steroid card. We’ll bring the dose down slowly once things settle — not all at once.
SCA_MODELS.why: Addresses the steroid fear honestly and weighs it against sight

SCA_MODELS.text: I’m also referring you today to the hospital’s rapid-access service for this condition. They aim to see people within a few days, often the same day, and they’ll arrange a scan or a small biopsy of the artery to confirm it. I’d like bloods today as well. Can you get to the surgery this afternoon?
SCA_MODELS.why: Arranges fast-track referral and same-day bloods alongside treatment

SCA_MODELS.text: I’d need someone to sit with my husband. I’m not sure who.
Let’s solve that together. Our team can look at who could help for the appointments, and I’d like to arrange a carer’s assessment so you have support if you’re unwell. Would that be okay?
SCA_MODELS.why: Builds the carer constraint into the plan so it happens

SCA_MODELS.text: Yes. I hadn’t thought about what happens if I’m the one who’s poorly.
That’s exactly why it matters. Staying well and keeping your sight is how you keep looking after him.
SCA_MODELS.why: Frames treatment as protecting her role as a carer

SCA_MODELS.text: The most important thing I’ll say today: if you get any change in your vision — blurring, double vision, or part of your sight going, even for a few minutes — that is an emergency. Call 999 or go straight to A&E and say you’re being treated for giant cell arteritis. Don’t wait to see if it passes.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific visual safety-net with an action and a phrase to use

SCA_MODELS.text: I understand. Any change in my eyes, 999.
Exactly. Never stop the steroid suddenly, and carry the card. I’ll ring you tomorrow to check you’ve started and to go through the bloods. Can you tell me back the three things you’re doing today?
Start the tablets, bloods this afternoon, and 999 if my eyes change. And the hospital will call.
Perfect. You did the right thing ringing. Anything else you wanted to ask?
SCA_MODELS.why: Checks understanding and shares the floor

SCA_MODELS.text: No, thank you, doctor. I’m glad I mentioned the headache now.

SCA_STEM.name: Eleanor Vance
SCA_STEM.recent: No recent bloods on record. No previous steroid prescriptions. Telephone request via reception: “something for the stiffness”.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone call: about 6 weeks of shoulder and hip stiffness; asking for a course of steroids.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: BSR GCA guideline (Mackie et al., 2020) · BSR/BHPR PMR guideline (Dasgupta et al., 2010) · NOGG 2024 · NatPSA/2020/005 Steroid Emergency Card · NICE NG243 (2024) · BNF
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Girdle pain and long morning stiffness at 72 fits polymyalgia, but a new headache, scalp tenderness and jaw pain on chewing mean suspected giant cell arteritis. Start high-dose prednisolone today and refer on the GCA fast-track pathway; tests must not delay treatment.

points.t: BSR/BHPR 2010: age over 50, bilateral shoulder and/or pelvic girdle aching with inflammatory morning stiffness for 2 weeks or more and raised inflammatory markers. Baseline bloods before steroids: FBC, ESR or CRP, U&E, LFT, bone profile, protein electrophoresis, TSH, CK, rheumatoid factor and urine dipstick. Isolated PMR starts at prednisolone 15 mg daily.

PMR and GCA overlap. Ask every patient with PMR symptoms about new headache (often temporal, one-sided), scalp tenderness, jaw or tongue claudication, visual disturbance and systemic upset. Jaw claudication is a high-risk feature.

BSR 2020: suspected GCA without visual loss — prednisolone 40–60 mg once daily, started by the GP the same day. Acute or intermittent visual loss — IV methylprednisolone (500 mg–1 g daily for up to 3 days) via same-day ophthalmology; do not delay oral steroid if IV is not immediately possible.

BSR 2020: refer urgently to the local GCA fast-track service — specialist review ideally the same working day and in all cases within 3 working days. Ultrasound of the temporal and axillary arteries (ideally before or within 72 hours of the first dose) and/or temporal artery biopsy (at least 1 cm), arranged urgently through the pathway, because steroids reduce test sensitivity. Tests must never delay treatment.

NOGG 2024: starting prednisolone 7.5 mg/day or more for 3 months or longer in a postmenopausal woman — start bone protection at the same time, without waiting for DXA. BSR 2020: gastroprotection according to GI risk, not routinely. NatPSA/2020/005: Steroid Emergency Card for 5 mg or more for 4 weeks or longer; sick-day rules per NICE NG243. Monitor glucose and BP. Never stop suddenly.

BSR 2020: hold the starting dose until symptoms and inflammatory markers have settled, then taper slowly to an individualised plan; the course commonly lasts 12–24 months. Symptoms usually respond within 1–7 days; no response should prompt a rethink.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question on the phone after an identity check; let her give the whole story, including the headache she dismissed.
Caring role for her husband with dementia; who covers him for appointments; the impact of the stiffness on daily tasks.
Picked up “a bit of a headache, neither here nor there” and turned it into specific GCA questions.
Idea (polymyalgia like her friend); concern (steroid side effects, being unable to care for her husband); expectation (a short course).
Same-day bloods (FBC, ESR/CRP, U&E, LFT, bone profile, glucose) without delaying steroids; fast-track referral for ultrasound or biopsy.
PMR alone versus PMR with GCA; PMR mimics (myeloma, other inflammatory arthritis) kept in mind.
Asked directly about scalp tenderness, jaw claudication and visual symptoms; knew visual loss means same-day ophthalmology and IV steroid.
Stated suspected GCA with PMR and explained it in plain words — sight is at risk, normal vision now is the window.
Prednisolone 40–60 mg started today (not the PMR dose), fast-track referral, bone protection, Steroid Emergency Card and a slow taper explained.
Hypertension and glucose monitoring on steroids; bone protection per NOGG 2024; gastroprotection considered; carer’s assessment offered.
Named visual symptoms as a 999 emergency, never stop steroids suddenly, and a GP call the next day.

social.t: She cares for her husband with dementia. Appointments, a possible biopsy and feeling unwell on treatment all need cover for him — plan it now or she will not attend.
Weight, mood, sleep and appetite change on high doses. Practical support and honest expectations improve adherence over a long taper.

legal.t: Any carer who appears to have support needs is entitled to a local authority carer’s assessment. Her husband can have a needs assessment and contingency planning if she becomes unwell.
No action needed while vision is normal. If GCA causes visual loss or a visual field defect, she must tell the DVLA and meet the Group 1 eyesight standard before driving.

professional.t: Starting high-dose steroid before confirmation is correct practice here (BSR 2020). Document the red flags, the dose, the referral and the safety-net advice given (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).
A phone call cannot examine the temporal artery or check acuity. Recognise the limit and bring examination and bloods forward the same day rather than deferring treatment.

community.t: PMRGCAuk (patient charity) for information and peer support; local carers’ centre and Carers UK; Dementia UK Admiral Nurses for her husband’s care planning.

redFlags: New one-sided headache, scalp tenderness, jaw or tongue claudication — suspected GCA
Any visual symptom (transient blurring, double vision, field loss) — same-day ophthalmology and IV steroid
Weight loss, night sweats, bone pain — consider PMR mimics such as myeloma
psychosocial: Sole carer for a husband with dementia — who covers him for appointments and if she is unwell
Steroid fears drawn from a friend’s experience and what she has read
Impact of the stiffness on dressing, washing and caring tasks
ice: Idea: “It’s polymyalgia, like my friend had.”
Concern: steroid side effects, and not being able to look after her husband
Expectation: a short course of steroids for the stiffness

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Be clear that this is suspected giant cell arteritis alongside polymyalgia: “The stiffness fits polymyalgia, but the headache, tender scalp and jaw ache point to inflammation in the arteries that can threaten your sight — so we treat it today.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of the blood vessels to your eye as a hosepipe that’s getting inflamed and narrowed. At the moment water is still getting through — your sight is fine. The steroid calms the inflammation before the hose is squeezed shut.”

management.reflectIce: “You were hoping for a short course, and you need to stay well for your husband. Treating this properly now is exactly what keeps you able to look after him.”
management.psychosocial: Arrange cover for her husband for the bloods and the specialist visit; offer a carer’s assessment and a contingency plan; give written steroid information to take away.
sharedPlan: Prednisolone 40–60 mg daily started today; fast-track GCA referral; same-day bloods
Bone protection, consider a PPI, Steroid Emergency Card, glucose and BP monitoring
Slow taper led by the specialist team; carer’s assessment and cover for appointments
safetyNet: Any visual change — 999 or A&E, say “giant cell arteritis”
Never stop steroids suddenly; sick-day rules; GP call tomorrow

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is not about knowing that GCA exists. It is failed on accepting the patient’s label, delaying steroids for tests, and ignoring the two things she is really worried about.

items.fail: Accepting “it’s polymyalgia” and prescribing 15 mg without asking about the headache.
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information to make a safe assessment.” She mentioned the headache once, then dismissed it — that is the test.
items.fix: Go back to it explicitly: side, newness, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual symptoms.

items.fail: Recognising GCA but waiting for ESR and CRP before starting steroids.
items.why: BSR 2020: start prednisolone 40–60 mg on clinical suspicion; tests must not delay treatment.
items.fix: “The steroid starts today; the tests follow.” Bloods the same day, and a fast-track referral.

items.fail: Starting high-dose steroid with no bone protection, steroid card or taper plan.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” NOGG 2024 advises bone protection from the start in this group; NatPSA/2020/005 requires a Steroid Emergency Card.
items.fix: Name bone protection, consider a PPI, give the card, and say the dose comes down slowly.

items.fail: Saying “don’t worry about side effects” when she raises moon face and bones.
items.why: “Does not respond to the patient’s concerns.” Brushing off an informed fear loses the trust needed for a year-long course.
items.fix: Acknowledge the downsides honestly, then weigh them openly against permanent loss of sight.

items.fail: Never returning to her husband after she mentions his dementia.
items.why: The carer role is why she is minimising. If nobody can sit with him, she will not attend.
items.fix: “Who could be with your husband this afternoon?” Offer a carer’s assessment and help with cover.

items.fail: A vague close — “ring us if things get worse”.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is standard failing feedback, and here it risks her sight.
items.fix: “Any change in your vision, even brief — 999 or A&E, and say giant cell arteritis.” Then teach-back and a dated call.
